name: Kansas Reflector
title: Task force dives into possible changes to Kansas school funding as current formula is set to expire
description: TOPEKA — A legislative committee resumed the challenging task this week of examining possible new school funding models to replace the one the state was forced to use by the courts.  Since 2016, the state has used a formula set after the settlement of a lawsuit that challenged the state for not fully funding education, […]
text:
Leah Fliter, assistant executive director of advocacy for the Kansas Association of School Boards, shown here testifyign in February, watched the Education Funding Task Force  with interest to track how possible changes to the public school funding formula would affect school districts statewide. (Kansas Reflector screen capture of Kansas Legislature video)TOPEKA — A legislative committee resumed the challenging task this week of examining possible new school funding models to replace the one the state was forced to use by the courts. 
Since 2016, the state has used a formula set after the settlement of a lawsuit that challenged the state for not fully funding education, said Leah Fliter, lobbyist at Kansas Association of School Boards.
With legislation that adopted the formula set to expire June 30, 2027, lawmakers are looking at how they can adjust the formula. 
The Education Funding Task Force considered more than 15 models with a variety of scenarios at its Tuesday and Wednesday meetings. Discussions ranged from pulling gifted education from special education funding to its own category to how weightings could be changed to support better literacy education in kindergarten through third grades.
Fliter said she watched the proceedings with interest to make sure the Legislature continues to fund at the current level. 
Task force members haven’t shown interest in cutting school funding overall, but the many models they considered would affect funding by school district whenever the formula changes, she said. Each district has different mixes of students with different needs. 
“Whenever you tweak the formula, you do end up with districts that gain money and districts that potentially lose money, so a winners-and-losers thing that plays out when you start to push and pull the levers and the buttons in the school formula,” she said. 
The “levers” are pieces of the funding formula that support services like special education, at-risk students and high or low enrollments. Each student gets base state aid and then, depending on extra needs, additional monies, Fliter said. 
“The formula was built to have these different weightings in place to to help make sure that everybody is getting an equitable and adequate education, regardless of where they live in the state,” Fliter said. 
The concept of whether a formula might lower or raise the amount school districts receive was one that caused disagreement within the task force. Rep. Nikki McDonald, D-Olathe, said she couldn’t foresee accepting a formula that gave any school districts fewer dollars than what they currently receive. 
Sen. Renee Erickson, R-Wichita, said any changes to the formula were certain to affect districts in a variety of ways. 
“The reality is that when we start making any change, no district is probably going to get exactly the same amount,” she said. “If that’s our goal, give everybody the same amount, then we just wasted two years of talking about what are some changes we can do better on the school finance formula.”
The current funding formula already has its own challenges, including how it accounts for inflation, Fliter said. Lawmakers in 2019 satisfied the Kansas Supreme Court by agreeing to automatically increase funding each year by the average increase in the Midwest consumer price index for the past three years.
“It was developed under a set of factors that really are no longer true,” she said. “They were not taking into account that inflation was going to do what it did, especially around the COVID pandemic.”
The inflationary adjustment doesn’t account for the actual increases in personnel costs, such as insurance and other benefits, Fliter said. 
The task force is scheduled to meet again in December.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: School funding reform could prompt constitutional convention, Greenwald says
description: Voters should approve eventual school funding reforms, the Assembly Majority Leader suggested during a panel discussion Wednesday.
text:
Assemblyman Lou Greenwald (D-Camden), pictured with Assemblywoman Eliana Pintor Marin (D-Essex), speaks about the $50.6 billion budget New Jersey lawmakers approved on June 29, 2022. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey should call a constitutional convention to include voters in the approval of a new school funding formula once a proposal is finalized, Assembly Majority Leader Lou Greenwald (D-Camden) said.
Though legislators and Gov. Mikie Sherrill in August began soliciting input for changes to the state’s funding formula, officials have said little about how their eventual proposal would differ from the funding formula enacted in 2008, and it’s not clear whether or how a formula enshrined in the state’s constitution would affect court precedent that demands New Jersey students receive a thorough and efficient education.
“I think ultimately this is going to need to lead to a constitutional convention and then a question that will include the voters as part of the solution because I think, ultimately at the end of the day, this is an issue that New Jersey has struggled with for generations,” Greenwald said Wednesday during a panel discussion at the New Jersey League of Municipalities’ annual conference.
In New Jersey, the state calculates how much each municipality must spend to provide their students a constitutionally sound education and how much those districts can raise on their own based on their residents’ incomes and property values.
State aid fills the rest, though not all districts raise enough revenue to meet the local spending — called a local fair share — needed to fully fund schools after state aid is added.
Some cannot raise enough revenue locally because of the state’s 2% cap on annual property tax levies, and others have been hammered by steep swings in state aid as the state in 2018 moved to begin phasing out aid meant to keep districts whole after the enactment of the 2008 funding formula.
At present, local governments in New Jersey look to property taxes to fund their share of school expenses, and Greenwald suggested that could change as a result of the yet-to-be-determined reforms.
“We need to understand that we are fixing a fundamentally broken tax system that dates back to the origins of this state as one of the founding states of this country,” Greenwald said.
New Jersey in 2024 tied with Illinois for the highest property tax rate in the nation, according to the Tax Foundation, and the average property tax bill in the state rose to a record high $10,570 last year.
It’s unclear what changes to the state’s funding formula lawmakers will eventually propose. The Department of Education last week said it would continue soliciting feedback from stakeholders at least through December.
Senate Majority Leader Teresa Ruiz (D-Essex) earlier told the Monitor she does not expect a proposal to be ready before the end of the current July-to-June fiscal year.
Among some other things, the reforms aim to better fund school transportation and extraordinary special education.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Data centers, teacher pay part of West Virginia Treasurer’s agenda
description: The West Virginia State Treasurer announced a packed agenda for the 2027 legislative session, saying he’ll be advocating teacher raises and reform to the data center law.
text:
West Virginia Treasurer Larry Pack, standing in front of the Treasurer Office’s vault, tells reporters about his agenda for the 2027 legislative session on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Photo by Henry Culvyhouse/West Virginia Watch)The West Virginia State Treasurer announced a packed agenda for the 2027 legislative session, saying he’ll be advocating teacher raises and reform to the data center law. 
Standing in front of the office’s vault, Treasurer Larry Pack said data center law, known by its bill number House Bill 2014, and education were top concerns he heard from residents across the state. 
“I’m just amazed that people know a House bill number and what it’s about,” Pack said. “That speaks to the controversy, that speaks to the magnitude of the bill that was passed a couple years ago.” 
Pack said he’ll be working with the Legislature to introduce legislation to reset how taxes are allocated, keeping property taxes for county commissions and school boards like any other economic development project. 
Pack said he had concerns that school districts weren’t getting a dime for data centers, because the current formulation sends most of the money to the state to be placed in an income tax reduction fund. 
“The money when it first comes in, goes in an account called personal income tax refunds,” Pack said. “ But before the year end is out, it’s just transferred to the general fund.” 
“But there’s nothing in 2014 that talks about a tax cut,” he continued. “There’s nothing in there that gives a tax cut to West Virginians in 2014. The money, the money when it first comes in, goes in an account called personal income tax refunds. But before the year end is out, it’s just transferred to the general fund.”
While Pack’s data center plan is focused on property taxation, he said he’s supportive of looking into wider reforms on data centers in West Virginia. 
“Data centers are bringing amazing opportunities to West Virginia in terms of jobs. In terms of investment, in terms of being able to use the fossil fuels and the oil and gas that we create in West Virginia,” Pack said. 
“But there’s no question that I believe there needs to be more transparency. There needs to be local input,” he said. “But we’re trying to just focus on the dollar portion of it.” 
For teachers, Pack said he’s pushing for a $50,000 floor for all teachers in the state and a $2,000 raise for those above the threshold. Pack also called for elimination of the “grid” — a matrix contained in state law that outlines the pay for teachers for each year of service. 
“We got to give local control. We have more ability to do what they want to do,” Pack said. 
However, under questioning from Bob Aaron, of WCHS, Pack didn’t really call for a locality pay structure for areas of the state like the Eastern Panhandle, which has long been hemorrhaging teachers to Virginia and Maryland for higher wages. 
“I think we need to come up with a system where every board, every county board of education can have their own pay scale,” Pack said. 
Other proposals from Pack include: 

A constitutional amendment to put a three-term limit on elected members of the Board of Public Works, which would include Pack’s office, the state auditor, the agricultural commissioner, the attorney general and the secretary of state. 
A constitutional amendment to eliminate the business inventory tax. Pack said this would cost the state $100 million and is different from the elimination of personal property business tax that voters rejected in 2022.  
Changing appointments to boards, which he said numbered around 100 throughout the state and are all appointed by the governor.  Pack said he would like to see around 10 boards be appointed by members of the wider Board of Public Works to offload that responsibility.
Sunset on tax credits. Pack said tax credits should be up for renewal by the Legislature every five years. 
Reform of unclaimed property. Pack said he wants to see the laws tightened to make sure the rightful owners of unclaimed property being held at the Treasurer’s Office can be returned.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming voters soundly rejected a major property tax cut. Here’s why.
description:
While voters don’t love taxes, many preferred a more targeted approach to property tax relief than Proposition 1 offered.
The post Wyoming voters soundly rejected a major property tax cut. Here’s why. appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
No county more soundly rejected Prop 1 — the sweeping statewide property tax cut — on Wyoming’s ballot this year than Niobrara, the least populated county in the nation’s least populated state.
Rep. JD Williams lives in Lusk, Niobrara’s county seat, and represents his home county along with neighboring Weston and Goshen counties. The Republican lawmaker, who frequently communicates with constituents via social media, describes his community bordering Nebraska and South Dakota as deeply conservative. 
That means residents are OK with paying their own way, he said. One way they do that is through special districts, which collect property taxes in exchange for providing services such as the senior center, fire department and weed and pest control.
Proposition 1 would have hit their special districts hard, which Williams called a “deal breaker.” 

Rep. JD Williams, R-Lusk, during the 2026 Wyoming Legislature budget session in Cheyenne. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)

“I would say that’s why Niobrara County rejected it at a higher percentage than any other county in the state,” he said. “Just because we are not interested in giving any more control, decision-making authority or taxing authority to the state of Wyoming, and that’s what it would have done.”
As Williams sees it, the ability to fund special taxing districts keeps power closer to home. 
“It would have moved local decision-making authority to the Legislature, away from local boards, specifically our county commission,” Williams said. 
On Nov. 3, Wyoming voters soundly rejected Prop 1, which received less than 42% support. Even in a deeply conservative state, only one county backed the measure: Lincoln County, with support from 57% of the voters. On the other end was Niobrara County, where less than 30% of voters wanted to enact this type of tax relief. 
WyoFile teamed with partner publications to examine why Wyoming’s disparate counties voted the way they did on Proposition 1. Also known as The People’s Initiative to Limit Property Tax in Wyoming through a Homeowner’s Property Exemption, the initiative landed on the Nov. 3 general election ballot with the backing of more than 30,000 valid signatures collected around the state. If passed, it would have exempted 50% of a primary residence’s assessed value from property taxation, causing Wyoming’s annual property tax revenues to drop.


The state’s first citizen initiative to land on the ballot in 30 years, Prop 1 needed approval from more than 50% of those voting in the general election to pass. 
Although many expected a close vote, the measure’s failure caught some by surprise. Along with a potential loss of local control and services, voters remained leery of Prop 1 for many reasons, including worries that it would raise other types of taxes, benefit Teton County billionaires and unleash unintended consequences. 
Lincoln County lone yes
While Niobrara County anchors Wyoming’s eastern flank, Lincoln County sits on the opposite side of the state, bordering Idaho. Former Rep. Marti Halverson, a Republican who represented northern Lincoln County and southern Teton County for six years, rallied for Prop 1 in the only county that ultimately supported it.
Halverson described her own community as split before Election Day. But in Star Valley, in the northern part of the county, she said, people “voted for it overwhelmingly enough to override the undervotes, overvotes and the no votes in Opal, Kemmerer, Diamondville, Frontier and Cokeville.”
In places like Star Valley, the real estate market caught fire amid the COVID-19 pandemic, as people from around the country escaped to rural communities. As buyers snapped up properties, home prices — and property tax bills — soared. 
“I have two close neighbors who saw their property taxes double,” Halverson said. “Now, these are working families with mortgages, and their mortgages went up $400 to $500 a month.” 
Looking north across Star Valley in northern Lincoln County on Sept. 6, 2026, from Salt River Pass. Average residential fair market value in Lincoln County jumped 186% from 2015 to 2025. (Ryan Dorgan/WyoFile)
The rise in property values varies widely across the state. Historical average residential fair market value jumped 257% (183% after exemptions) and 186% (116%) in Teton and Lincoln counties respectively, the two highest increases, followed by Sheridan at 109% (48%). In contrast, Niobrara saw a 44% increase, which dropped to just 6% once tax exemptions were applied, during the same period from 2015 to 2025, according to a Legislative Service Office analysis. Campbell and Big Horn counties saw similar increases of 65% (12%) and 67% (19%), respectively during the same period.
State lawmakers heard homeowners’ concerns and responded with a slew of new and expanded tax breaks. But Prop 1 supporters saw more room to cut. While disappointed Prop 1 didn’t pass, Halverson said she “wasn’t surprised with over $2 million being spent against it.” 
Property tax vs. sales, income tax
The initiative’s failure has given Halverson “hope” that talk of increasing sales tax or imposing a state income tax is now “off the legislative table.” 
“I don’t think with the failure of Prop 1 that the Legislature can, in good conscience, raise any taxes,” she said. 
The risk that sales tax or a state income tax could eventually backfill revenue lost from the property tax cut drove some of the opposition to Prop 1. 
Tom Harrington spearheaded “Concerned Citizens of Big Horn County,” a group that rallied against Prop 1, waving signs at motorists traveling through Shell Canyon in north central Wyoming every Sunday for about six weeks ahead of the election. He shares Halverson’s desire to avoid sales and income taxes.
“I’m against both of them, especially the sales tax, which is regressive and will unfairly impact the lower income people in our community,” Harrington said. “And income tax, I think, is just anathema to Wyoming, and I don’t think that’ll ever fly.” 
Harrington served as a judge in Big Horn, Hot Springs and Washakie counties before retiring. These days he helps out with the Greybull and Basin wrestling program. He still sees room for targeted property tax reform, especially for longtime Wyoming residents and specifically, single people, be they widowers or widows on fixed incomes and over age 65. 
But he saw Prop 1 as a chainsaw approach that would damage local services.
Likewise, Steve Helburn voted against Prop 1, in part, because of potential cuts to libraries, Meals on Wheels and law enforcement. He also didn’t like that the “benefit was primarily for the billionaires in Teton County, and little benefit to much less benefit to other parts of the state.” 


The Greybull resident already qualifies for property tax relief as a veteran and senior who has paid property taxes for more than 25 years in Wyoming. “I can get both of those,” Helburn said. “I don’t always, but they’re available to me.” 
Harrington also qualifies for existing tax relief programs, and has used them in the past. But he’s considering not applying in the future to support local services. 
The Wyoming Taxpayers Association, which opposed Prop 1, estimated that Big Horn County alone had lost more than $2 million in revenue from 2025 tax exemption programs, excluding the veteran’s exemption and refund and deferral programs. Had Prop 1 passed, the association estimated the county could have lost nearly $1.9 million more.
Big Horn County Commissioner Bruce Jolley, a Lovell Republican, also qualifies for the relatively new exemptions. But Jolley typically opts instead for the veterans discount because it doesn’t pinch the county budget since the state reimburses the county for that relief program, he said. Gov. Mark Gordon included $16.6 million to extend property tax relief programs in his supplemental budget announced Monday.
Jolley fielded many calls from constituents asking his position on Prop 1, which he opposed. Most were concerned about the county, towns, schools and special districts losing funding, Jolley said. “I see firsthand how it affects the budget of the county.” 
He’s also leery of one tax cut opening the door to raising other types of taxes.  
“I am especially against any kind of tax backfill because that means our sales tax will rise, which in northern Wyoming, especially in Washakie, Hot Springs and Big Horn counties, that is going to directly affect our small business,” he said. “More people will utilize the option of going to Montana to buy their goods and services.”
Tax-rich county declines cut
In the county with the highest property tax values in Wyoming, voters not only opposed giving themselves a property tax break this general election but also decided to increase taxes for the local hospital and maintain a tax for environmental conservation.
Roughly 63% of Teton County voters opposed Prop 1. Some voters coming out of the polls Nov. 3 were conflicted.
“I ultimately voted against it,” Austin O’Bryhim, 33, said. “Not because I don’t agree with property tax relief — because I think in this county, specifically, it’s well needed — but they did not demonstrate the ability to make up for that budget deficit elsewhere.”
The estimated financial impact was significant. The Wyoming Department of Revenue and Legislative Service Office estimated there could be roughly $109 million to $125 million exempted from residential property tax bills statewide in the first year. In Teton County alone, nearly $37 million could have been exempted, according to the Wyoming Taxpayers Association.
Residential property tax dollars don’t go to the state’s general fund, but rather to public education and local governments. Roughly two-thirds of residential property taxes pay for Wyoming schools. The remaining one-third funds county government such as administration, roads and general operations; special districts, including fire protection, hospital districts, weed and pest control and water/sewer; and city and town budgets, according to the revenue department.
Voters arrive to cast ballots in the general election Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at the Old Wilson Schoolhouse in Teton County. (Bradly J. Boner/Jackson Hole News&Guide)
Margo Krisjansons, who has lived in Teton County since 1973, also voted against property tax relief.
“I’m a little guy. I’m not a billionaire,” Krisjansons said, “so I got to think about the long-term for what’s good for me as a homeowner in Kelly.”
The death of Prop 1 took some Teton County voters like Republican Werner E. Minshall by surprise. He’s frustrated by the lack of overarching tax relief, and although he said he could afford his high tax bill at around $36,000, others couldn’t.
“It’s extremely unfortunate,” Minshall said about Prop 1 failing. “So, now we’re going to have a bloated government in Teton County.”
Big Horn County conservatives, who also supported Prop 1, blamed scare tactics for its failure. 
“I believe that it’s humanitarian in the way that it helps families that are buying property, families that are trying to hold on to property and older folks and even regular folks trying to pay their bills,” said Gordon Preis, a Republican committeeman who lives in Emblem. Preis joined other conservative voters in Big Horn County to buy an advertisement in the Greybull Standard urging fellow citizens to support Prop 1.
“The real issue is they don’t want to lose their tax money, the state, the county,” Preis said. 
Preis compared it to how he pens his cows, getting them a little hungry and then leading them into the pen. “People fall into the trap every time.”
‘Prop 1’ splits two ways in Campbell County
Campbell County voters were close to evenly split on the ballot initiative. After Lincoln and Park counties, Campbell County came the closest to passing Prop 1. That it failed, winning about 48% of the vote, shocked many in a county where mineral taxes bankroll many services. Minerals generate about 78% of Campbell County’s property tax revenue.
Even though he opposed Prop 1, Campbell County Commissioner and former Republican legislator Scott Clem said it’s hard to say why the initiative didn’t pass.
“Being able to pay less (in property tax) is certainly appealing,” Clem said. “I still wonder how much the public is aware about the tax remedies that have been implemented in the past couple of years.”
Campbell County Commissioner Scott Clem poses for a portrait in downtown Gillette on Nov. 11, 2025. (Jonathan Gallardo/Gillette News Record)
Only 40% of eligible Campbell County taxpayers have applied for the relatively new exemptions for the 2026 tax year, Assessor Erin Slattery wrote in an email. The other 60% may choose to pay property taxes to fund local services or not know their options. 
Governments can do a better job informing taxpayers about existing tax exemptions and relief options, Clem said.
Gillette real estate agent Josh McGrath gave multiple presentations about initiatives called Prop 1. There was Prop 1, the statewide initiative.
But Campbell County also had its own local Prop 1, asking voters to renew a penny sales tax to fund local services for another four years. The penny tax was promoted in Gillette with signs of Abraham Lincoln, reminding voters the local tax funds more than $18 million in infrastructure, maintenance, public safety and other programs around town. 
While the statewide initiative failed, voters renewed the penny tax by nearly 68%. 
Messaging from Campbell County groups combined with campaigning from outside organizations, such as the Wyoming Taxpayers Association, could have impacted the results, McGrath said.
“I think it’s because they saw the benefit of the (penny tax), and I think that maybe had a bit of a residual effect. Like, ‘Hey, I’ve seen what this has done as a benefit,’” McGrath said. “They’re both named Prop 1, but I don’t have a great reason for why it’s split. It was one of those hot topics where you’re either for it or against it, and there’s not any middle ground.”
Wanda Lieneman was a regional campaign manager for Cody Republican Brent Bien’s gubernatorial run and helped gather some of the more than 30,000 signatures for the initiative he helped get on the ballot. She pointed to negative ads from groups like the Wyoming Education Association and Wyoming Taxpayers Association as the biggest reason it didn’t pass. 
She called the results of her petition work “devastating.” Lieneman started working on the initiative after seeing friends get taxed out of their homes, she said. Her own property tax bill on her home has more than doubled in the past five years, but she takes advantage of the 50% exemption for seniors.
She disagreed that local services would suffer, suggesting local governments could be supported by interest income generated from the state’s and other rainy day funds. Revenue for school districts, law enforcement and other public services doesn’t have to come from property taxes, she said. 
Lieneman said Prop 1 could be the last time Wyoming residents see a ballot initiative like it.
“What can I do? We did everything we could to get it through, and the lies went out that we were not telling people the truth,” Lieneman said. “I’m going to continue to fight for it, I’ll go down to the Legislature and do my part there, but as far as the initiative goes, it’s dead.”
For Commissioner Clem, a lack of relief for renters and the potential for unintended consequences added to the list of reasons he voted against Prop 1. 
“All taxes suck. No one likes them, not even me, but they are a necessary evil for a functioning 21st Century society,” he said. “In this case, the devil you know is better than the devil you don’t know.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Commentary: Kentucky missed the tax trigger. Here’s how to hit it.
description: For the second consecutive year, and the third time in four years, Kentucky has failed to meet the revenue benchmarks required to further cut the state income tax. The shortfall this time wasn’t even close, as General Fund receipts fell short of the threshold needed. Kentucky’s new tax regime has cut the personal income tax […]
text:
In January, at a pro-housing rally, Sen. Robby Mills, R-Henderson, said bills to tackle the housing shortage should be moving soon in the Kentucky legislature. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)For the second consecutive year, and the third time in four years, Kentucky has failed to meet the revenue benchmarks required to further cut the state income tax. The shortfall this time wasn’t even close, as General Fund receipts fell short of the threshold needed.
Kentucky’s new tax regime has cut the personal income tax rate from 5 percent to 3.5 percent. In an analysis for the Bluegrass Institute, Rea Hederman Jr. and Sai Martha found that reaching 3 percent would add $810 million in GDP and $370 million in private investment in its first year, and by 2034 would generate $850 million in annual investment and 7,000 new jobs. Our large rainy day fund and the healthy General Fund surplus confirm that Kentucky is not spending recklessly; this means the problem is on the growth side of the ledger.
The commonwealth’s competitors aren’t slowing down. Iowa, Louisiana and Idaho cut individual income tax rates in 2025, and this year Montana did. Both Mississippi and South Carolina have enacted revenue-triggered phase-outs aimed at eliminating the income tax, and Oklahoma has cut its rate with triggers for future cuts.
Senator Chris McDaniel, R-Ryland Heights, chairman of the budget committee, said Kentucky’s miss this year demonstrates the “responsibility” and “reactiveness” of the model. He’s clearly right on the first count, but reactiveness is the wrong posture for a state that has set elimination of its income tax as a long-term goal. Kentucky needs a proactive growth agenda that expands the tax base by making the commonwealth a better place to start a business, build a home, and earn a living.
Three simple reforms, none of which require new spending, would accomplish exactly that.
 Cut the red tape
Kentucky’s regulatory code contains more than 127,000 restrictive requirements spread across 6.4 million words. Between 2020 and 2024, the commonwealth’s regulatory burden grew 8.8 percent – double the national median of 4.4 percent. Every one of those restrictions is a barrier between a would-be entrepreneur and satisfied customers.
Patrick McLaughlin of the Hoover Institution, writing for the Bluegrass Institute, documented what happens when states take this problem seriously. When British Columbia cut its regulatory burden by 40 percent, GDP growth surged. Virginia’s 25 percent reduction saves residents an estimated $1.2 billion a year. McLaughlin’s model projects that a 20% cut in Kentucky would leave Kentucky’s economy roughly $14 billion larger by 2037.
Frankfort should begin with a systematic review of the commonwealth’s administrative code by adopting regulatory transparency, identifying rules that are no longer useful and sunsetting them. The Bluegrass Institute’s own research finds that even a 10% reduction in restrictions would raise growth. The General Assembly should give regulatory reform the same priority as income tax reduction – the two are indelibly connected.
 Let Kentuckians build
People follow opportunity, and homes are where jobs go to sleep at night. In the Lexington and Bowling Green housing markets, median home prices are near historic highs relative to household income, pricing out workers and families Kentucky needs to attract.
The cause is not a lack of demand, it is a thicket of mostly local regulations – minimum lot sizes, parking mandates, and permitting timelines that stretch months past any reasonable review period. This artificially constrains supply. The Bluegrass Institute’s “Menu of Options for Kentucky Housing Reform” lays out a detailed deregulatory agenda: permitting shot clocks, by-right approval of accessory dwelling units and small multifamily buildings, elimination of arbitrary lot-size minimums and adoption of the “Golden Girls Rule” that lets unrelated adults share a home without local government meddling.
Virginia’s regulatory streamlining, which included simplifying housing rules, is projected to cut roughly $24,000 from the cost of a new home. More homes mean more property tax revenue, more construction jobs, more appliance and furniture sales, and more families putting down roots in Kentucky communities, which all show up in General Fund receipts.
Here in Kentucky, lawmakers failed to deliver on housing affordability when the omnibus housing bill died in the final hours of the 2026 session. This is in spite of the fact that the Kentucky Housing Task Force, co-chaired by Sen. Robby Mills and Rep. Susan Tyler Witten, embraced many Bluegrass Institute recommendations that would expand housing supply at no cost to taxpayers. Too often, the legislature has substituted new government programs like trust funds, loan subsidies, and tax credits for the genuine deregulation that would let the market build. The next session should finish what the task force started.
 Open the door
Kentucky requires a government license to work in 132 of 246 occupations tracked by the Archbridge Institute, making us the ninth-most-burdensome licensing regime in the US. The Institute for Justice’s License to Work report finds that Kentucky licenses 38 of 102 lower-income occupations it studied, ranking the commonwealth 13th in licensing burden for the workers who can least afford it.
Research suggests occupational licensing reduces employment by up to 27 % in licensed fields. It is a barrier that keeps people out of the labor force, and is exactly the opposite of what a state trying to grow its tax base should do. Kentucky’s July unemployment rate was 4.7%, above the national average of 4.1%. Neighboring Indiana, which licenses fewer occupations, had an unemployment rate of 3.3%. Correlation is not causation, but the pattern is worth examining.
Every barber, auctioneer, florist and massage therapist who is deterred from working in Kentucky by months of mandatory training, hundreds of dollars in fees and exams that test academic knowledge rather than practical competence is a taxpayer the commonwealth never gains.
The Bluegrass Institute has identified occupational licensing reform as a key move to improve Kentucky’s economic freedom. Kentucky ranks in the bottom half of states on the Fraser Institute’s economic freedom index and is the second-most federally dependent state in the nation. Reducing licensing barriers is one of the fastest ways to change both numbers.
 The path forward
Kentucky’s income tax trigger mechanism was designed to ensure that tax cuts are undertaken by a stable government with dependable revenues, not revenues borrowed from future taxpayers. But missing the trigger year after year should not be treated as an acceptable outcome; it should be treated as a policy signal that Kentucky’s private sector is not growing fast enough.
The General Assembly reconvenes in January. Lawmakers who are serious about finishing what HB 8 started should arrive in Frankfort with an agenda that matches their ambition. The path to zero runs through a bigger, freer Kentucky economy.

title: Virginia lawmakers weigh using marijuana taxes to fund school substance use programs
description: Virginia lawmakers on Monday discussed using future marijuana tax revenue to expand substance use prevention and counseling in public schools, after a new survey found that few secondary schools screen students for substance use risks or have specialized counselors.  The Joint Commission to Oversee the Transition of the Commonwealth into a Cannabis Retail Ma[...]
text:
Virginia lawmakers are weighing whether to use tax revenue from future retail marijuana sales to expand substance use prevention and counseling in public schools. (Photo by Getty Images)Virginia lawmakers on Monday discussed using future marijuana tax revenue to expand substance use prevention and counseling in public schools, after a new survey found that few secondary schools screen students for substance use risks or have specialized counselors. 
The Joint Commission to Oversee the Transition of the Commonwealth into a Cannabis Retail Market learned that just 13% of secondary schools surveyed in September use formal screening to identify students at risk, while about one in five have a substance use counselor.
Del. Cia Price, D-Newport News, urged the state to help schools pay for screening, evidence-based prevention programs and alternatives to suspension while the Virginia Department of Education studies staffing needs and costs. 
“I don’t want to wait until 2028 to find out that we should have done something this year,” Price said. 
Virginia is preparing to launch legal retail market sales July 1, 2027. A briefing by the Behavioral Health Commission projected that the forthcoming state retail cannabis tax of 6% to 8% could generate $11.3 million in fiscal 2028, rising to $74 million by fiscal 2032. 
The money would be divided among several designated purposes, including K-12 education and substance use prevention and treatment through community service boards. The joint commission is responsible for recommending how the revenue should be spent. 
 Schools struggle to intervene early

John Barfield, a policy analyst for the Behavioral Health Commission, told lawmakers that youth substance use has declined over the long term and that Virginia generally fares better than the national average. 
But vaping on school grounds remains a concern, he said, particularly as nicotine concentrations in vaping products and THC potency in marijuana have increased. 
Virginia schools already cover substance use in health classes. Yet only 11% of elementary schools and 29% of secondary schools represented in the survey of school counselors reported combining classroom instruction with evidence-based prevention programs and community partnerships. 
Barfield said research shows that approach has the strongest lasting effect on student behavior.
Formal screening could also help identify students who need intervention before their problems worsen. According to Barfield, research shows universal screening identifies more than twice as many at-risk students as informal methods such as staff observation.
Some schools, however, expressed concern that screening could reveal more students needing help than their staff could accommodate. 
“I think the concern, in many instances, is, if we discover that a significant portion of our students have a problem and we don’t have the resources to address that problem, where does that leave us?” Barfield said. “Counselors or nurses could screen students and refer those at highest risk for services.”
Del. Katrina Callsen, D-Albemarle, said screening could also give parents information to help address problems at home. Barfield said parental consent would be required. 
The survey found that about a quarter of responding secondary schools offered diversion programs as alternatives to suspension. 
Price tied that finding to testimony the commission heard in September from RISE for Youth, which warned that increasing penalties for public marijuana use could place additional financial burdens on families. 
State data cited by the group showed that marijuana-related juvenile intake complaints declined 30% from fiscal 2019 to fiscal 2024, even as the share originating in schools rose from 17% to 54%. 
“About 60% of responding secondary schools partnered with an outpatient provider, usually a community services board,” Barfield said. “About a third brought clinicians into schools, easing transportation and scheduling barriers.” 
 Getting money to school divisions

The Behavioral Health Commission has adopted recommendations to fund a new position at the Virginia Department of Education in the 2027 budget, assess school divisions’ substance use prevention and treatment needs by Dec. 1, 2027, and conduct follow-up surveys every two years beginning in 2028. 
Barfield estimated the new position would cost about $120,000. The employee would help school divisions select evidence-based programs, train staff and put prevention efforts into practice. 
Asked what could help schools sooner, Barfield pointed to certified substance use counselors.
“They seem to be, based on our site visits, kind of the glue that holds all of it together, and they have the capacity to go out and make those community partnerships,” he said. “They have the capacity to kind of identify those evidence-based programs, and they have the necessary training to do early intervention really well.”
Virginia has no dedicated funding stream for substance use services in schools, Barfield said. 
Much of the existing support comes from grants, while general state education funding helps pay for school counselors who often handle substance use concerns alongside their other responsibilities. 
Nathalie Molliet-Ribet, executive director of the Behavioral Health Commission, suggested providing every school division with a baseline allocation to support at least one employee focused on substance use. 
She said competitive grants can put less-resourced divisions at a disadvantage because they may lack the staff needed to prepare applications. 
Sen. Lashrecse Aird, D-Henrico, who chairs the commission, asked how lawmakers could make sure divisions spend the money on the intended services. 
Molliet-Ribet suggested defining eligible expenses and requiring divisions to report how they used the funding. 
Del. Will Morefield, R-Tazewell, cautioned against requiring local governments to hire additional employees without providing enough state money to cover the costs. 
“The majority of rural counties, especially in the area that I represent, just simply can’t afford to take on another position,” Morefield said. 
Other states already direct marijuana tax revenue toward education and substance use services, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. 
Colorado has used marijuana revenue to fund grants that help schools to hire behavioral health professionals. 
Molliet-Ribet said members of the Behavioral Health Commission would introduce the budget amendments needed to carry out their recommendations. 
Aird said the joint commission could also put forward its own recommendations as lawmakers prepare for the 2027 legislative session, which begins Jan. 13.
